newsitem.title: USA: Clinton calls Mexico move a good step against drugs.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls Mexico move a good step against drugs.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Thursday that Mexico's decision to dismantle its scandal-marred anti-drug agency was a "good first step" but that the Mexicans still faced a big challenge fighting drugs.
Clinton commented in a radio interview as he prepared to make a state visit to Mexico on Monday as part of a week-long Latin American tour that will also include stops in Costa Rica and Barbados.
It will be his first trip to America's southern neighbour since he became president in 1993 even though Mexico is one of America's largest trading partners.

Clinton and other U.S. officials were optimistic on the drug war a day after Mexican Attorney General Jorge Madrazo Cuellar announced that the dismantled agency would be replaced by a new body of trained agents who would be screened on a regular basis.
The new agency, the Special Prosecutor's Office for Crimes Against Health, is to begin work immediately. Drug offences are termed crimes against health in Mexico.

The new agency replaces the National Institute for Drug Combat (INCD), which fell under a cloud when its chief, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, was arrested in February and charged with taking bribes from Mexico's most wanted drug lord, Amado Carrillo Fuentes.
"I think there's a good chance that it will improve things. Keep in mind the Mexicans have a big challenge," Clinton told CNN Radio Noticias in an interview. "I think this is a very good first step."
Presidential aides were also positive, but cautionary.
"I think this is a government that understands the problem, understands the threat," said National Security Adviser Sandy Berger.
But he also said: "Is there corruption in the Mexican system? I think that President Zedillo would be the first to acknowledge that there is."

The U.S. drug czar, retired Gen. Barry McCaffrey, said that based on the murders in the line of duty of many Mexican police officers, plus 25 major assassinations, "there is no question that their democratic institutions are under attack from within."
He said he expected that the United States and Mexico would achieve some "incremental agreements" on the war against illegal drugs during Clinton's trip.

Washington has put heavy pressure on Mexico in recent years to root out drug corruption and stop narcotics smuggling across the border. But despite constant pledges and new programmes, anti-drug agents say the flow of cocaine, marijuana and heroin continues hardly checked.
